claim: osl-dynamics is a Python-based package that can identify and describe recurrent dynamics in functional neuroimaging data on timescales as fast as tens of milliseconds.
source: Here, we present the OHBA Software Library Dynamics Toolbox (osl-dynamics), a Python-based package that can identify and describe recurrent dynamics in functional neuroimaging data on timescales as fast as tens of milliseconds.
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract as a description of the toolbox's capabilities.

claim: osl-dynamics incorporates machine learning generative models that can adapt to the data and learn the timing, spatial and spectral characteristics of brain activity with few assumptions.
source: At its core are machine learning generative models that are able to adapt to the data and learn the timing, as well as the spatial and spectral characteristics, of brain activity with few assumptions.
evidence: Stated in the abstract describing the core methodology of the toolbox.

claim: osl-dynamics can be used with magneto/electroencephalography, functional magnetic resonance imaging, invasive local field potential recordings, and electrocorticography data.
source: osl-dynamics incorporates state-of-the-art approaches that can be, and have been, used to elucidate brain dynamics in a wide range of data types, including magneto/electroencephalography, functional magnetic resonance imaging, invasive local field potential recordings, and electrocorticography.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as the range of applicable data modalities.

claim: Neural oscillations have been linked to cognitive processes such as information encoding and processing, as well as attention.
source: Neural oscillations have been linked to cognitive processes, such as information encoding and processing, as well as attention (Ward, 2003) and distinct oscillatory activity has been observed in different states of consciousness (Engel and Fries, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ward, 2003.

claim: Synchronization of neural oscillations has been proposed as a mechanism for communication.
source: Furthermore, the synchronization of neural oscillations has been proposed as a mechanism for communication (Fries, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fries, 2015.

claim: Changes in oscillatory activity have been observed between diseased and healthy cohorts.
source: Neural oscillations have also been a useful tool for understanding brain dysfunction; for example, changes have been observed in the oscillatory activity of diseased and healthy cohorts (Başar and Güntekin, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Başar and Güntekin, 2008.

claim: Neuronal populations exhibit short bursts of oscillatory activity on timescales of 100 ms.
source: Recently, it has been proposed that neuronal populations exhibit short bursts of oscillatory activity on timescales of 100 ms (Jones, 2016; Shin et al., 2017; Seedat et al., 2020) rather than the classical view of ongoing oscillations that are modulated in amplitude.
evidence: Supported by citations to Jones, 2016; Shin et al., 2017; Seedat et al., 2020.

claim: Oscillatory bursting can occur across cortical networks.
source: It has been shown that bursting can occur across cortical networks (Seedat et al., 2020), and there are bursts of coherent activity in networks that last on the order of 50–100 ms in both resting-state (Vidaurre et al., 2018b) and in task (Quinn et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Seedat et al., 2020; Vidaurre et al., 2018b; Quinn et al., 2018.

claim: The dynamics of specific functional resting-state networks have been linked to memory replay, a process that occurs in memory consolidation on timescales of ≤50 ms.
source: Precise knowledge of these fast network dynamics is a valuable insight that can help us understand cognitive processes; for example, the dynamics of specific functional resting-state networks have been linked to memory replay (a≤50 ms process that occurs in memory consolidation) (Higgins et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Higgins et al., 2021.

claim: Changes in the dynamics of functional networks have been shown to be predictive of behavioral traits.
source: Changes in the dynamics of functional networks have also been shown to be predictive of behavioral traits (Liégeois et al., 2019) and disease (Sitnikova et al., 2018; Du et al., 2018; Van Schependom et al., 2019; Salvan et al., 2021; Sharma et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liégeois et al., 2019.

claim: Changes in the dynamics of functional networks have been shown to be predictive of disease.
source: Changes in the dynamics of functional networks have also been shown to be predictive of behavioral traits (Liégeois et al., 2019) and disease (Sitnikova et al., 2018; Du et al., 2018; Van Schependom et al., 2019; Salvan et al., 2021; Sharma et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sitnikova et al., 2018; Du et al., 2018; Van Schependom et al., 2019; Salvan et al., 2021; Sharma et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2020.

claim: A three-state TDE-HMM can identify oscillatory bursts in a data-driven fashion without requiring pre-specification of frequency, amplitude threshold, or duration.
source: Instead of a conventional burst detection method, we use a three state TDE-HMM to identify bursts in a data-driven fashion.
evidence: Demonstrated in the burst detection results (Section 2.1) where the TDE-HMM identifies bursts without pre-specified parameters.

claim: Oscillatory bursts identified by the TDE-HMM have lifetimes ranging from a hundred to several hundred milliseconds.
source: We can see from Figure 1BIV that these bursts have a variety of lifetimes ranging from a hundred to several hundred milliseconds.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1BIV and stated in the text.

claim: The AE-HMM identifies plausible functional networks including a default mode network, two visual networks, frontotemporal networks, and a sensorimotor network.
source: We see the AE-HMM identifies plausible functional networks (Buckner et al., 2011) with fast dynamics, typically with lifetimes of around 50 ms (Figure 2AIII). We identify a default mode network (state 1); two visual networks (states 2 and 6); a frontotemporal networks (states 3 and 7); and a sensorimotor network (state 4).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2AI and described in the text, with citation to Buckner et al., 2011 for plausibility.

claim: The functional networks identified by the AE-HMM have fast dynamics with lifetimes of around 50 ms.
source: We see the AE-HMM identifies plausible functional networks (Buckner et al., 2011) with fast dynamics, typically with lifetimes of around 50 ms (Figure 2AIII).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2AIII and stated in the text.

claim: Visual networks show significant activation (p<0.05) between 50-100 ms after presentation of visual stimuli in the Elekta task MEG dataset.
source: We observe a significant increase (p<0.05) in the activation of the visual networks (states 2 and 6) between 50–100 ms after the presentation of the visual stimuli as expected.
evidence: Shown in Figure 2BI with statistical testing.

claim: A frontotemporal network shows significant activation (p<0.05) 300-900 ms after visual stimuli presentation.
source: We also observe a significant activation (p<0.05) of the frontotemporal network (state 7) 300–900 ms after the visual stimuli as well as a deactivation of the visual networks (states 2 and 6).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2BI with statistical testing.

claim: The TDE-HMM identifies networks with distinct spectral (oscillatory) activity.
source: We can see from the state PSDs (Figure 3AI, bottom) that the networks identified by the TDE-HMM exhibit distinct spectral (oscillatory) activity.
evidence: Shown in Figure 3AI bottom panel.

claim: The TDE-HMM power maps show the same spatial patterns as the AE-HMM amplitude maps for high-power networks.
source: For the high-power networks (states 1–4), we see the same spatial patterns in TDE-HMM power maps (Figure 3AI, top) and AE-HMM amplitude maps (Figure 2AI).
evidence: Comparison between Figure 3AI and Figure 2AI.

claim: The TDE-HMM networks have fast dynamics with lifetimes of around 50 ms.
source: The TDE-HMM networks also have fast dynamics (Figure 3AIII) with lifetimes of around 50 ms.
evidence: Shown in Figure 3AIII.

claim: Similar networks are observed in rest and task MEG data.
source: We observe similar networks in rest (Figure 4A) as in task (Figure 3A), which is a known result from fMRI studies (Smith et al., 2009).
evidence: Comparison between Figure 4A and Figure 3A, with citation to Smith et al., 2009.

claim: Regions with high power activations have high connectivity (coherence) in the TDE-HMM networks.
source: We observe regions with high power activations have high connectivity (coherence).
evidence: Observed in Figures 3AI and 4AI showing coherence networks.

claim: The fractional occupancy of the sensorimotor network (state 4) is significantly increased (p<0.05) in older participants (34-60 years) compared to younger participants (18-34 years).
source: We see the fractional occupancy and switching rate of the sensorimotor network (state 4) is increased in the older group (p<0.05).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4BI with statistical testing.

claim: The switching rate of the sensorimotor network (state 4) is significantly increased (p<0.05) in older participants compared to younger participants.
source: We see the fractional occupancy and switching rate of the sensorimotor network (state 4) is increased in the older group (p<0.05).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4BI with statistical testing.

claim: The mean lifetime of the visual network (state 6) is significantly decreased (p<0.05) in older participants compared to younger participants.
source: The mean lifetime of the visual network (state 6) is also decreased in the older group (p<0.05).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4BI with statistical testing.

claim: The older group has a wider distribution of mean intervals (p<0.05) for the default mode network (state 1) and suppressed state (8).
source: The older group also has a wider distribution of mean intervals for the default mode network (state 1) and suppressed state (8) (p<0.05).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4BI with statistical testing.

claim: DyNeMo identifies more localized power activations and cleaner network structure than the TDE-HMM.
source: We can see from the power maps and coherence networks (Figure 5AI) that DyNeMo identifies much more localized power activations and a cleaner network structure than was seen with the TDE-HMM.
evidence: Comparison between Figure 5AI and Figure 4AI.

claim: DyNeMo networks exhibit distinct spectral characteristics.
source: We can see from the PSDs (Figure 5AI, bottom) that these networks also exhibit distinct spectral characteristics.
evidence: Shown in Figure 5AI bottom panel.

claim: DyNeMo describes brain activity as overlapping networks that dynamically vary in mixing ratios.
source: From the (renormalized) mode time course (Figure 5AII) we see the description provided by DyNeMo is that of overlapping networks that dynamically vary in mixing ratios.
evidence: Shown in Figure 5AII and described in the text.

claim: Modes with activity in neighboring regions show more co-activation in DyNeMo.
source: We observe modes with activity in neighboring regions show more co-activation.
evidence: Observed in Figure 5AIII showing mode correlations.

claim: DyNeMo shows an increased mode contribution (p<0.01) for the sensorimotor network (mode 4) in older participants compared to younger participants.
source: We can see an increased mode contribution (mean renormalized mode time course) for the sensorimotor network (mode 4), which reflects the increase in fractional occupancy we saw in the TDE-HMM (Figure 4BI). We see DyNeMo is able to reveal a stronger effect size with a p<0.01 compared to the TDE-HMM, which had a p<0.05.
evidence: Shown in Figure 5BI with statistical testing.

claim: DyNeMo shows a decrease in variability (p<0.01) for the left temporal network (mode 5) in older participants compared to younger participants.
source: DyNeMo also shows a decrease in the variability (standard deviation of the renormalized mode time course) for the left temporal network (mode 5, p<0.01).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5BI with statistical testing.

claim: The TDE-HMM is less sensitive to amplitude and better able to identify low-amplitude oscillatory bursts compared to conventional amplitude thresholding methods.
source: In contrast, the TDE-HMM is less sensitive to the amplitude (it is better able to identify low-amplitude oscillatory bursts) and can identify the frequency of oscillations automatically.
evidence: Discussed in the context of burst detection advantages.

claim: The TDE-HMM can identify the frequency of oscillations automatically without pre-specification.
source: In contrast, the TDE-HMM is less sensitive to the amplitude (it is better able to identify low-amplitude oscillatory bursts) and can identify the frequency of oscillations automatically.
evidence: Discussed in the context of burst detection advantages.

claim: The TDE-HMM can model dynamics in oscillatory amplitude and phase synchronization whereas the AE-HMM can only model dynamics in amplitude.
source: The TDE-HMM approach is able to model dynamics in oscillatory amplitude and phase synchronization whereas the AE-HMM can only model dynamics in amplitude.
evidence: Stated as a comparison between the two methods.

claim: The HMM assumes mutually exclusive network states.
source: The HMM assumes that there are mutually exclusive network states, whereas DyNeMo assumes the network modes are mixed differently at each time point.
evidence: Stated as a fundamental difference between HMM and DyNeMo.

claim: DyNeMo assumes network modes are mixed differently at each time point.
source: The HMM assumes that there are mutually exclusive network states, whereas DyNeMo assumes the network modes are mixed differently at each time point.
evidence: Stated as a fundamental difference between HMM and DyNeMo.

claim: DyNeMo uses richer temporal regularization through a deep recurrent network compared to the HMM.
source: DyNeMo does have the additional advantage of using a richer temporal regularisation through the use of a deep recurrent network. This has been shown to capture longer-range temporal structure than the HMM (Gohil et al., 2022), and exploring the cognitive importance of long-range temporal structure is an interesting area of future investigation (van Es, 2023).
evidence: Stated with citation to Gohil et al., 2022.

claim: DyNeMo has been shown to capture longer-range temporal structure than the HMM.
source: This has been shown to capture longer-range temporal structure than the HMM (Gohil et al., 2022), and exploring the cognitive importance of long-range temporal structure is an interesting area of future investigation (van Es, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gohil et al., 2022.

claim: osl-dynamics is an open-source package written in Python.
source: We present a new toolbox for studying time series data: osl-dynamics. This is an open-source package written in Python.
evidence: Stated in the Conclusions section.

claim: Using Python avoids the need for a paid license.
source: We believe the availability of this package in Python improves the accessibility of these tools, in particular for non-technical users. Additionally, it avoids the need for a paid license.
evidence: Stated as an advantage of using Python.

claim: Using Python enables osl-dynamics to take advantage of modern deep learning libraries, particularly TensorFlow.
source: Using Python also enables us to take advantage of modern deep learning libraries (in particular TensorFlow, 2023) which enables us to scale these methods to very large datasets, something that is currently not possible with existing toolboxes.
evidence: Stated as an advantage with citation to TensorFlow, 2023.

claim: The sliding window approach for calculating time series properties suffers from a tradeoff between temporal precision of dynamics and accurate estimation of properties.
source: However, this approach only utilizes a short window around the time point of interest and suffers from a tradeoff between the temporal precision of dynamics and an accurate estimation of the properties (via a sufficiently large window).
evidence: Stated as a limitation of the sliding window approach.

claim: The sliding window approach is inadequate for studying fast changes in functional connectivity.
source: In Liuzzi et al., 2019, it was shown that this approach is inadequate for studying fast changes in functional connectivity.
evidence: Supported by citation to Liuzzi et al., 2019.

claim: Generative models can identify non-contiguous segments of time series that share the same latent variable, leading to more robust estimates of local properties.
source: In doing this, the model can identify non-contiguous segments of the time series that share the same latent variable. Pooling this information leads to more robust estimates of the local properties of the data.
evidence: Stated as an advantage of the generative model approach.

claim: The HMM uses variational Bayesian inference to learn the most likely state to have generated the observed data.
source: osl-dynamics uses variational Bayesian inference Bishop and Nasrabadi, 2006 to learn the most likely state to have generated the observed data.
evidence: Stated in the description of the HMM with citation to Bishop and Nasrabadi, 2006.

claim: Variational Bayesian inference has the advantage of being able to account for uncertainty in the latent state.
source: This has the advantage of being able to account for uncertainty in the latent state.
evidence: Stated as an advantage of variational Bayesian inference.

claim: The HMM has been successfully used to study dynamics in neuroimaging data in a variety of settings.
source: The HMM has been successfully used to study dynamics in neuroimaging data in a variety of settings (Seedat et al., 2020; Khawaldeh et al., 2022; Vidaurre et al., 2018b; Quinn et al., 2018; Higgins et al., 2021; Sitnikova et al., 2018; Van Schependom et al., 2019; Vidaurre et al., 2016; Vidaurre et al., 2018a; Vidaurre et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: DyNeMo overcomes two key limitations of the HMM: mutually exclusive states and limited memory.
source: DyNeMo is a recently proposed model that overcomes two key limitations of the HMM: the mutually exclusive states and limited memory (Gohil et al., 2022).
evidence: Stated with citation to Gohil et al., 2022.

claim: DyNeMo uses amortized variational Bayesian inference to learn the most likely latent vector to have generated the observed data.
source: osl-dynamics uses amortized variational Bayesian inference Kingma and Welling, 2013 to learn the most likely latent vector to have generated the observed data.
evidence: Stated in the description of DyNeMo with citation to Kingma and Welling, 2013.

claim: Amortized variational Bayesian inference is a highly efficient inference scheme that is scalable to large datasets.
source: This is a highly efficient inference scheme that is scalable to large datasets.
evidence: Stated as an advantage of amortized variational Bayesian inference.

claim: Time-delay embedding augments the time series with extra channels containing time-lagged versions of the original channels.
source: This augments the time series with extra channels containing time-lagged versions of the original channels.
evidence: Stated in the description of TDE.

claim: Time-delay embedding embeds the autocorrelation function of the original data into the covariance matrix of the TDE data.
source: By adding extra channels, we embed the autocorrelation function (ACF) of the original data (as well as the cross-correlation function) into the covariance matrix of the TDE data.
evidence: Stated in the description of TDE and illustrated in Figure 9CII.

claim: Using TDE data makes the covariance matrix sensitive to the frequency of oscillations in the original data.
source: By using TDE data we make the covariance matrix sensitive to the frequency of oscillations in the original data.
evidence: Stated in the description of TDE.

claim: Training on TDE data allows study of dynamics in oscillatory amplitude and phase synchronization between channels.
source: Training on TDE data allows us to study dynamics in oscillatory amplitude and phase synchronization between channels.
evidence: Stated as the purpose of using TDE data.

claim: The HMM and DyNeMo are trained by minimizing the variational free energy cost function.
source: The HMM and DyNeMo are trained by minimizing a cost function (in osl-dynamics, we use the variational free energy Rezek and Roberts, 2005; Gohil et al., 2022).
evidence: Stated in the description of training with citations to Rezek and Roberts, 2005; Gohil et al., 2022.

claim: The HMM and DyNeMo training can converge to different explanations of the data due to local optimum issues.
source: As is typical, this approach suffers from a local optimum issue, where the model can converge to different explanations (latent descriptions) of the data during training.
evidence: Stated as a limitation of the training approach.

claim: A strategy for dealing with run-to-run variability is to train multiple models and analyze only the model with the lowest variational free energy.
source: A strategy for dealing with this that has worked well in the past is to train multiple models from scratch (each model is referred to as a run) and only the model with the lowest variational free energy is analyzed.
evidence: Stated as a strategy used in the manuscript.

claim: The best run from a set of 10 consistently finds the same set of model parameters.
source: Empirically, we find picking the best run from a set of 10 consistently finds the same set of model parameters.
evidence: Stated as an empirical finding.

claim: The age-related differences observed in the young vs old comparison are consistent with existing studies.
source: The age-related differences we observe here are consistent with existing studies (Coquelet et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Coquelet et al., 2020.

claim: An increase in static power could be due to more frequent activations of a particular network.
source: The static (time-averaged) differences we see in young vs old participants can arise in many ways from the underlying dynamics of resting-state networks (Figures 4AI and 5AI). For example, an increase in static power could be due to more frequent activations of a particular network.
evidence: Stated as a possible explanation for static differences.

claim: Static differences in power may arise from altered power within a network while the dynamics of the networks remain unaffected.
source: Conversely, the dynamics of the networks may be unaffected and the power within a network could be altered.
evidence: Stated as an alternative explanation for static differences.

claim: The HMM's stronger assumption of mutually exclusive states simplifies the decomposition and can make interpreting network dynamics more straightforward.
source: While DyNeMo's assumption is arguably more realistic, the HMM's stronger assumption has the benefit of simplifying the decomposition, which can make interpreting the network dynamics more straightforward.
evidence: Stated as a comparison between HMM and DyNeMo.

claim: The HMM and DyNeMo provide complementary descriptions of network dynamics.
source: In short, the HMM and DyNeMo provide complementary descriptions of network dynamics, with either one being potentially useful depending on the context (Gohil et al., 2022).
evidence: Stated with citation to Gohil et al., 2022.

claim: A better performance in a downstream task indicates a more useful model.
source: It is possible to quantify which model is better using a downstream task. In this manuscript, the downstream tasks are the evoked network response and young vs old group differences. We argue a better performance in the downstream task indicates a more useful model.
evidence: Stated as a criterion for model evaluation.

claim: osl-dynamics can compute static network descriptions using the same methodology as state or mode specific network estimation in dynamic approaches.
source: osl-dynamics can also be used to compute static network descriptions, including conventional static functional connectivity. This uses the same methodology as the state (or mode) specific network estimation in the dynamic approaches, making comparisons between dynamic and static perspectives more straightforward.
evidence: Stated as a feature of the toolbox.

claim: The HMM has been validated on simulated data for burst detection applications.
source: Both the HMM and DyNeMo have been validated on simulated data for each application. See Quinn et al., 2019 for a demonstration of the HMM's ability to identify oscillatory bursts and Vidaurre et al., 2016; Gohil et al., 2022 for a demonstration of the HMM/DyNeMo's ability to identify dynamic networks.
evidence: Supported by citation to Quinn et al., 2019.

claim: The HMM and DyNeMo have been validated on simulated data for identifying dynamic networks.
source: Both the HMM and DyNeMo have been validated on simulated data for each application. See Quinn et al., 2019 for a demonstration of the HMM's ability to identify oscillatory bursts and Vidaurre et al., 2016; Gohil et al., 2022 for a demonstration of the HMM/DyNeMo's ability to identify dynamic networks.
evidence: Supported by citations to Vidaurre et al., 2016; Gohil et al., 2022.

claim: The burst detection approach assumes bursting is being looked for in a single channel (brain region) at a time.
source: This approach assumes that we are looking for bursting in a single channel (brain region) at a time; separate HMMs can be used to detect bursting in each channel.
evidence: Stated as an assumption of the burst detection approach.

claim: The multitaper approach is used to calculate PSDs due to its ability to accurately estimate spectra.
source: We use the multitaper approach described in Vidaurre et al., 2016 to do this due to its ability to accurately estimate spectra.
evidence: Stated with citation to Vidaurre et al., 2016.

claim: Principal component analysis is often needed after TDE for dimensionality reduction to ensure data fits into computer memory.
source: This means after TDE we have a very large number of channels (number of embeddings times the number of regions). Therefore, we often need to perform principal component analysis (PCA) for dimensionality reduction to ensure the data fits into computer memory.
evidence: Stated as a practical necessity in the TDE-HMM pipeline.

claim: Non-negative matrix factorization is applied to stacked subject and state-specific coherence spectra to identify common frequency bands of coherent activity.
source: Note that we also use the spectral decomposition approach introduced in Vidaurre et al., 2018b to specify a frequency range for calculating power maps and coherence networks. This involves applying non-negative matrix factorization to the stacked subject and state-specific coherence spectra to identify common frequency bands of coherent activity.
evidence: Stated with citation to Vidaurre et al., 2018b.

claim: The GLM-based approach is used to calculate mode and region-specific PSDs in DyNeMo by regressing mixing coefficients onto a cross spectrogram.
source: To calculate mode and region-specific PSDs, we use the approach based on the General Linear Model (GLM) proposed in Quinn et al., 2022a where we regress the mixing coefficients onto a (cross) spectrogram, see Gohil et al., 2022 for further details.
evidence: Stated with citations to Quinn et al., 2022a and Gohil et al., 2022.

claim: The mode time course in DyNeMo does not contain information regarding the relative magnitude of each mode covariance.
source: Note that an additional complication related to the mode time course is that it does not contain any information regarding the relative magnitude of each mode covariance.
evidence: Stated as a complication in interpreting DyNeMo results.

claim: The mode time course is renormalized by weighing each mode time course by the trace of its mode covariance.
source: We account for this by renormalizing the mode time course (We weigh each mode time course by the trace of its mode covariance and divide by the sum over modes at each time point to ensure the renormalized mode time course sums to one), this is discussed further in Gohil et al., 2022.
evidence: Stated with citation to Gohil et al., 2022.

claim: A two-component Gaussian Mixture Model can be used to binarise DyNeMo mode time courses to calculate HMM-like summary statistics.
source: Alternatively, if we were interested in calculating the same summary statistics as the HMM (fractional occupancy, lifetime, interval, switching rate) we would first need to binarise the mode time courses. This can be done using a two-component Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM), which is discussed in Gohil et al., 2022.
evidence: Stated with citation to Gohil et al., 2022.

claim: A two-component GMM is used to threshold networks by fitting to the distribution of connections, with one component representing background connections and the other representing atypically strong connections.
source: In this work, we will specify the threshold using a data-driven approach where we fit a two-component GMM to the distribution of connections in each network. We interpret one of the components as the distribution for background connections and the other as the distribution for atypically strong connections, which is what we display in each plot.
evidence: Stated as the thresholding method used.

claim: For static networks, the top 5% of connections are displayed rather than using the GMM thresholding approach.
source: Note, for the static networks we select the top 5% of connections to display in each plot rather than the GMM approach we used to threshold the dynamic functional networks.
evidence: Stated as the thresholding method for static networks.

claim: Different state/mode time courses can lead to similar values for the variational free energy.
source: As is typical, this approach suffers from a local optimum issue, where the model can converge to different explanations (latent descriptions) of the data during training. That is, different state/mode time courses can lead to similar values for the variational free energy.
evidence: Stated as a characteristic of the training process.

claim: The final description from HMM/DyNeMo training can be sensitive to the stochasticity in updating model parameters and the initial parameter values.
source: The final description can be sensitive to the stochasticity in updating model parameters and the initial parameter values.
evidence: Stated as a source of variability in training.

claim: Results are deemed reproducible if the same model parameters are consistently inferred from a dataset.
source: We deem a set of results as reproducible if we are consistently able to infer the same model parameters from a dataset.
evidence: Stated as the criterion for reproducibility.

claim: For a given set of hyperparameters, only the relative difference between values for the variational free energy is important.
source: Note, for a given set of hyperparameters, only the relative difference between values for the variational free energy is important.
evidence: Stated as a note about interpreting variational free energy.
